clue.text: Live amongst enemies in French resort

indicators.note: amongst says the word for live sits among the letters of the enemies

parts.note: antis are people against something, opponents
to be is to live or exist

explanation.surface: A traveller settles down among hostile people on the Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live' looks like an adjective but is the verb, giving BE; 'amongst' signals the container. Antibes lies on the French Riviera.
explanation.definitionFit: Antibes is a well-known seaside town on the Côte d'Azur, so it is an example of a resort in France.

clue.text: Gather together about 500 potential customers

indicators.note: about says the gathering word goes around the Roman numeral

parts.note: to amass is to collect or gather together
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: A salesman rounds up about five hundred likely buyers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts D inside AMASS.
explanation.definitionFit: The admass is the mass public targeted by advertising, the consumers it hopes to win.

clue.text: Not like novel's author

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new order

explanation.surface: The writer of a book is unlike anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel's' looks like part of the definition, but 'novel' rearranges NOT LIKE.
explanation.definitionFit: J. R. R. Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings, so he is a famous writer.

clue.text: Not a single woman healthy in this prison

parts.note: a bride is a woman marrying, so no longer single
well means healthy

explanation.surface: A married woman stays fit while in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridewell was a London prison, and the name came to mean any house of correction.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridewell is an old term for a jail or house of correction, named after the London one.

clue.text: Prudish artist getting drunk with added spirits

indicators.note: getting drunk suggests the word artist reels about into a new order

parts.note: a drink laced with something has had alcohol added

explanation.surface: A painter who drinks spiked drinks is still prim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting drunk' makes STRAIT, and 'laced' drinks are spiked with spirits; strait here is the old word for narrow or tight, as in tightly laced corsets.
explanation.definitionFit: Strait-laced describes someone rigidly proper and easily shocked, puritanical.

clue.text: A little maiden caught amidst hatred

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

indicators.note: amidst places the cricket letter in the middle of the word for hatred

parts.note: odium is intense dislike or hatred
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A girl is caught up in a small amount of loathing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amidst' puts C inside ODIUM, after M.
explanation.definitionFit: A modicum is a small quantity, a tiny portion of something.

clue.text: Relative silence

explanation.surface: Mother says nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Mum is a mother, a family member, and 'mum' also means silent, as in 'keep mum'.

clue.text: Allow delay, provided extra fare is raised

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means the letters go upward, read bottom to top

parts.note: refed means fed again, given more food

explanation.surface: Let a hold-up happen, so long as the surcharge on the ticket goes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'provided' looks like 'if' but means fed; 'is raised' turns REFED upward.
explanation.definitionFit: To defer is to postpone, letting something be put off.

clue.text: Meat consumed by company is antelope

indicators.note: consumed by means the meat word is swallowed inside the company abbreviation

parts.note: ham is a meat
taken as written

explanation.surface: A firm eats meat that comes from a horned animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumed by' signals the container; CO for company is a standard abbreviation, and the chamois lives in the Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: The chamois is a goat-antelope of European mountains.

clue.text: I'd confused airmen about line between poles

indicators.note: confused shows the letters of the following words are muddled up

explanation.surface: A pilot admits the crew got lost about the route north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges I'D AIRMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A meridian is a line of longitude running from the North Pole to the South Pole.

clue.text: Damage measure I'm backing a tiny amount

indicators.note: backing tells us the words for damage and I'm are read from right to left

parts.note: ill can mean harm or damage, as in 'do him no ill'
taken as its letters I and M
a gram is a unit of measure of weight

explanation.surface: Someone claims to support a small sum while doing harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns the damage and I'm pieces into MILLI, even though the measure sits between them in the clue; the measure is then tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: A milligram is one thousandth of a gram, a minute weight.

clue.text: Aptitude of learner in moderate set

indicators.note: in places the learner's letter inside the word for moderate

parts.note: fair can mean middling or moderate, as in 'fair to middling'
L is the learner, as on a British learner driver's L-plate

explanation.surface: A pupil in a middling class shows some talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set' completes the surface: L is set in FAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair is a natural talent or knack for something.

clue.text: It may be appropriate to strike

explanation.surface: Something that might be suitable for hitting.
explanation.definitionFit: To swipe is slang for stealing (appropriating something), and also to hit with a sweeping blow.

clue.text: American author is that female Shaw joined

parts.note: taken as written
her is the pronoun for that female
a shaw is an old word for a small wood or thicket

explanation.surface: A writer from the US is that woman George Bernard Shaw married.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaw' looks like the playwright; it is the old word for a copse.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Isherwood, British-born, took US citizenship and wrote novels in California, so he counts as an American writer.

clue.text: Eminent drunk ran over top man

parts.note: high can mean intoxicated
taken as written
a king is the man at the top

explanation.surface: A distinguished drunk knocked down the boss.
explanation.definitionFit: High-ranking means of senior status, prominent.

clue.text: Smart set? Fashionable and elegant list I prepared

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in 'the in thing'

indicators.note: prepared signals that the letters are made ready in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Stylish people? A polished guest list has been drawn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' makes TELLIGENTSIA; the question mark warns that 'Smart set' means the brainy set, not the fashionable one.
explanation.definitionFit: The intelligentsia are the intellectual class, the clever people of a society: 'smart' read as brainy.

clue.text: Gloominess mostly dissipated in new term

indicators.note: dissipated suggests scattering, so the letters are dispersed into a fresh order
mostly means the word is cut short of its final letter

explanation.surface: Melancholy mostly lifts at the start of a new school session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last S of GLOOMINESS; 'dissipated' rearranges GLOOMINES.
explanation.definitionFit: A neologism is a newly coined word or expression.

clue.text: Traditional Liberal in opposite of 15

indicators.note: in places the Liberal abbreviation inside the phrase

parts.note: the reverse of a newly made word is a long-established one

explanation.surface: A traditional Liberal stands against new ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 is NEOLOGISM, a new word, so its opposite is OLD WORD; 'in' puts L inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Old-world means old-fashioned and quaint, belonging to former times.

clue.text: Minor form of punishment for exiled leader

parts.note: little means minor or small
corporal punishment is physical punishment, so corporal names that form

explanation.surface: Smacking a child is a lesser kind of discipline for a banished ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: The Little Corporal was the nickname of Napoleon, exiled to Elba and then St Helena.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon Bonaparte, nicknamed this, was a ruler sent into exile, so the nickname names a banished leader.

clue.text: Lawyer one found in order to protect pilgrims

definitions.text: one found in order to protect pilgrims

explanation.surface: A barrister belongs to a religious order guarding travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: A Templar is a barrister of the Inner or Middle Temple in London, and the Knights Templar guarded pilgrims to Jerusalem.
explanation.definitionFit: Templar names a lawyer of London's Temple and a knight of the medieval military order that escorted pilgrims.

clue.text: Royal Academy elite assembled in studio

indicators.note: assembled means the letters are put together in a new arrangement

parts.note: RA is the abbreviation for the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: The top members of the Royal Academy gathered in an artist's workroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assembled' rearranges RA and ELITE.
explanation.definitionFit: An atelier is an artist's or designer's workshop.

clue.text: Ancient vessel initially bringing one part of army

indicators.note: initially picks the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a corps of the British Army

explanation.surface: An old ship first brings one unit of soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A bireme was an ancient galley with two banks of oars.

clue.text: Commonplace sporting event

explanation.surface: An ordinary, everyday sports fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonplace' looks like 'ordinary', but means a place with a common: Wimbledon Common in south-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Wimbledon is a London district famous for its common, a place with a common, and also the tennis championship held there.

clue.text: Supply article in French city

indicators.note: in puts the article inside the name of the city

parts.note: Lyon is a large city in France
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Delivering a newspaper piece in Lyon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts A inside LYON.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay on is to provide or arrange something, such as food or transport.

clue.text: Daggers carried by Shinto believers

indicators.note: carried by means the letters are held within the run of the following words

explanation.surface: Weapons are borne by followers of a Japanese faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeli are dagger symbols used in printing to mark references, also called obelisks.

clue.text: Annoy unknown person enjoying carefree existence

parts.note: to rile is to annoy or irritate
Y is a mathematical unknown, like X

explanation.surface: An unidentified person living without cares annoys others.
explanation.walkthrough: From the phrase 'the life of Riley', an easy, carefree life.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'living the life of Riley' makes the name stand for someone with an easy, untroubled lifestyle.

clue.text: Original Rousseau, for example

explanation.surface: Rousseau is cited as a first-hand source.
explanation.walkthrough: Henri Rousseau, the self-taught French painter, is a classic example of a naive or primitive artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Primitive means earliest or original, and it also labels a naive, untrained painter like Henri Rousseau.

clue.text: Author's unfinished literary work

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', a link to the wordplay

indicators.note: unfinished means the last letter of the work is cut off

parts.note: a poem is a literary work

explanation.surface: A writer's piece of literature is not yet complete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' drops the M from POEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer of poems and tales of mystery.

clue.text: Old-fashioned imprisonment current in France

explanation.surface: An outdated form of jail is the present practice across the Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current' looks like 'present-day' but means a river: the Durance flows in south-east France.
explanation.definitionFit: Durance is an archaic word for confinement in prison, and also a river of Provence.

clue.text: Stick old actor in difficult position up here

parts.note: gum is glue, something that makes things stick
Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree was a celebrated Victorian actor-manager

explanation.surface: Glue an elderly thespian into an awkward spot.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'up a gum tree' is British slang for being in a fix, so the tree is where the predicament lies.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'up a gum tree' means in trouble, so the eucalyptus is the place one is stuck in that plight.
